content: 1. Promethazine HCl Syrup Plain can impair mental and physical abilities required for performing potentially hazardous tasks, such as driving or operating machinery. This impairment may be exacerbated by the concurrent use of other central nervous system depressants, including alcohol, sedatives, hypnotics (e.g., barbiturates), narcotics, narcotic analgesics, general anesthetics, tricyclic antidepressants, and tranquilizers. Therefore, these agents should either be avoided or administered in reduced dosages when used alongside Promethazine HCl. 2. Promethazine HCl Syrup Plain has the potential to cause severe and potentially fatal respiratory depression. It should be avoided in patients with conditions that predispose them to respiratory compromise, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or sleep apnea. 3. Promethazine HCl Syrup Plain may lower the seizure threshold. It should be used cautiously in individuals with seizure disorders or those taking medications that may also affect the seizure threshold, such as narcotics or local anesthetics. 4. Promethazine HCl Syrup Plain should be used with caution in patients with bone marrow depression. Cases of leukopenia and agranulocytosis have been reported, particularly when Promethazine HCl is used in combination with other known marrow-toxic agents. 5. Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS), a potentially fatal condition, has been reported in association with Promethazine HCl, either alone or in combination with antipsychotic drugs. Clinical manifestations of NMS include hyperpyrexia, muscle rigidity, altered mental status, and signs of autonomic instability, such as irregular pulse or blood pressure, tachycardia, diaphoresis, and cardiac dysrhythmias. 6. Diagnosing NMS can be challenging, as it requires differentiation from other serious medical conditions, such as systemic infections, pneumonia, untreated extrapyramidal symptoms, central anticholinergic toxicity, heat stroke, drug fever, or primary CNS pathology. 7. Management of NMS involves immediate discontinuation of Promethazine HCl, antipsychotic drugs, and any other non-essential medications. Intensive symptomatic treatment, medical monitoring, and addressing any concurrent serious medical conditions are also necessary. There is no consensus on specific pharmacological treatment regimens for uncomplicated NMS. 8. Recurrence of NMS has been reported with phenothiazines. Therefore, reintroducing Promethazine HCl should be approached with caution. 9. Promethazine HCl Syrup Plain is contraindicated in pediatric patients under two years of age due to the risk of fatal respiratory depression. Caution is advised when administering it to pediatric patients aged two years and older, as respiratory depression and apnea, sometimes resulting in death, have been strongly associated with Promethazine products. These effects are not directly related to weight-based dosing. 10. The concurrent use of Promethazine products with other respiratory depressants in pediatric patients has been associated with respiratory depression and, in some cases, death. 11. Antiemetics, including Promethazine HCl, are not recommended for treating uncomplicated vomiting in pediatric patients. Their use should be limited to prolonged vomiting of known etiology, such as encephalopathy or Reye’s syndrome. Promethazine HCl should be avoided in pediatric patients with signs or symptoms suggestive of Reye’s syndrome or other hepatic diseases. 12. Excessively large doses of antihistamines, including Promethazine HCl, in pediatric patients may result in sudden death. Hallucinations and convulsions have been reported with therapeutic doses and overdoses of Promethazine HCl in pediatric patients. Acutely ill pediatric patients with dehydration are at increased risk of dystonias when using Promethazine HCl. 13. Administration of Promethazine HCl has been associated with cases of cholestatic jaundice.
